content: Asthma is characterized by variable airflow obstruction accompanied by symptoms such as wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing. Its prevalence is increasing globally, particularly in higher-income countries. In several of these nations, there has been a shift toward managing asthma through primary care-based asthma clinics. These clinics provide structured, proactive asthma care within primary care settings, typically through regular, dedicated sessions led by nurses with support from doctors. The care provided in these clinics often includes systematic recall of patients listed on an asthma register, patient education, symptom assessment, and management based on established clinical guidelines. Despite the growing number of such clinics, especially in countries like the United Kingdom, there is limited evidence to substantiate their effectiveness. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy of asthma care delivered through primary care-based asthma clinics. To conduct this review, researchers searched the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register of trials (last updated in December 2011) and examined reference lists of primary studies for additional relevant trials. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a parallel group design, where the intervention involved asthma clinics operating during dedicated time slots with face-to-face interactions between patients and either a doctor or nurse. The control groups received standard care from general practitioners. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion and performed data extraction and analysis. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion. Ultimately, three studies involving a total of 466 participants met the inclusion criteria. The results showed no statistically significant differences between the asthma clinic group and the control group for most primary and secondary outcomes. Primary outcomes included asthma exacerbations leading to hospitalizations or visits to accident and emergency (A&E) departments, use of reliever and preventer medications, and quality of life. Secondary outcomes included symptom control, time lost from work, and withdrawal rates from the intervention or usual care. However, the confidence intervals for all outcomes were wide, and there was considerable variability between studies, particularly for A&E visits and time lost from work. One study, which included 101 participants, specifically examined nocturnal awakenings caused by asthma. This study found a statistically significant reduction in the number of patients reporting nocturnal symptoms in the asthma clinic group compared to the usual care group (odds ratio 0.31; 95% confidence interval 0.12 to 0.77). None of the included studies evaluated the secondary outcome of asthma exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the efficacy of primary care-based asthma clinics is limited. The findings do not allow for definitive conclusions, and further high-quality trials are necessary to establish their effectiveness.
